::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 12) you can:

1. **construct** a leakage-proof link prediction setup: message vs supervision edges, temporal vs random splits, negative sampling for evaluation, and metrics chosen to match the deployment (Hits@K/MRR vs AUC);
2. **derive** the VGAE objective — GCN encoder, inner-product decoder, reparameterization, ELBO — and implement it;
3. **explain** SEAL's enclosing-subgraph + labeling-trick idea, and prove why plain node embeddings cannot express what it expresses;
4. **describe** autoregressive generation (GraphRNN's ordering and RNNs) and diffusion-based generation (DiGress, at architecture level), and evaluate generated graphs by distribution statistics;
5. **articulate** where generation matters — molecules, synthetic data, anonymization — and what its evaluation cannot see.
:::

## The week a model scored 0.363

Every predictive week of this course has assumed the graph. Nodes carried
the labels to guess; the edges were simply *given* — the stage, never
the play. But run
through what the applications actually ask: recommend a product (predict a
user–item edge), suggest a collaborator (author–author edge), flag a
missing interaction (drug–protein edge — Week 5's toy KG was this task in
miniature), complete a knowledge base (Week 4's whole enterprise),
resolve duplicate records (an is-the-same-entity edge), warn about a
likely fraud connection before it consummates. Half of applied graph ML
is **link prediction** — the graph predicting its own missing parts — and
you have, in fact, already done it twice without the name: Week 3's
walk-embedding link experiment (where we measured the famous +17-point
leak) and all of Weeks 4–5's KG completion, which is link prediction with
typed edges. What this week adds is the *general* discipline those
special cases hinted at, plus the strongest modern architecture for it.
And then a second, stranger industry: **graph generation** — molecules
designed atom by atom, synthetic networks for testing and privacy — where
the model's output is not a score but a graph. This week is both, and its
through-line is the discipline this course has been rehearsing since Week
1, because no task punishes sloppy evaluation like the task where *the
labels are edges*.

Here is the week's cautionary artifact, measured on our own hardware
before a single method is introduced. We implemented SEAL — this week's
strongest link predictor — and made one small mistake: when building each
candidate pair's subgraph we removed the target edge from the *edge list*
but computed the node's distance labels from adjacency sets that still
contained it. Training positives thereby carried a tiny signature ("my
endpoints are adjacent") that test positives — whose edges were properly
held out — could not have. The model found it, leaned on it, and scored
**AUC 0.363 on test: reliably worse than flipping a coin**, because the
feature it trusted votes exactly backwards on honest data. One line of
labeling code separated 0.897 from 0.363. Not "the model underperformed" —
the model *anti-performed*, which is leakage's most theatrical failure
mode and its most diagnostic: mere uselessness scores 0.5, while a
confidently wrong model has learned something real about the *wrong
world*. This lecture hands you the checklist that catches it before the
leaderboard does.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Before any neural network: on our Cora test
split, how well does the dumbest possible link predictor — count the
common neighbors of the candidate pair — score in AUC? And will the
best learned model this week beat it by 5 points or by 20?

::: {.predict-answer}
Common neighbors alone: **AUC 0.724** (Adamic–Adar's weighting adds
one-thousandth: 0.725). The best learned models reach ~0.90 — an
eighteen-point gap, real but humbling in both directions: a zero-parameter
formula from Week 2 gets three-quarters of the way, and any paper that
compares its GNN only against random guessing is hiding this floor from
you. First lesson of the week: *the heuristic ladder is the baseline, not
the coin.*
:::
:::

## The split is the method

Node classification could afford casual splits; link prediction cannot,
because edges play two roles at once — they are the *medium* (messages
flow along them) and the *label* (their existence is what we predict). An
edge must never play both roles at once for the same example. The
professional setup therefore gives every edge exactly one job:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w12-splits.html >}}

::: {#def-w12-buckets .definition name="The four-bucket link split"}
Partition the edges into four buckets, one job each. **Message edges**
build the graph the encoder propagates over — visible always.
**Supervision edges** are training positives: the loss pushes their
scores up, but they are *not in the message graph*. **Validation** and
**test edges** are invisible to everything until their moment — and
"everything" is a longer list than it sounds: not in the message graph,
not among training pairs, not inside any precomputed feature, not
reachable by any walk the pipeline ever takes. Read the split as a row
of one-way mirrors: each bucket is seen only by the stages its card
names, and every leak in this lecture violates exactly one card.
:::

Why supervision edges must leave the message graph: an edge that both
carries the messages and is the thing being predicted gives the encoder
a one-hop tautology ("are these nodes linked? let me ask the link") —
the model reads its answers off the blackboard. In practice many
pipelines let message and supervision coincide for training positives
and accept the softer, train-only distortion; the strict separation is
the honest default, it is what Lab 12 builds, and the difference between
the two conventions is one of the first things to check when two papers'
VGAE numbers disagree by a point.

Three rules complete the contract. Test edges must be absent from the
message graph — Week 3 measured this exact leak at +17 AUC points when
walks crossed held-out edges. Negatives are sampled from *non-edges of
the full graph* (a "negative" that is secretly a test positive corrupts
the exam — Week 4's accidentally-true negatives, returning). And
heuristics compute on the message graph only: common neighbors counted
on the full graph is leakage wearing a formula.

Audit yourself on the toy version — the widget's starting state is the
single most common real-world bug:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w12-split.html >}}

Concretely, our own split this week — the one every measured number in
this lecture shares: Cora's 5,278 undirected edges shuffled once with a
fixed seed into 527 test positives (10%), 263 validation, and 4,488
training positives, the training positives doubling as the message
graph; 527 test negatives sampled from non-edges with their own seed.
Every method — heuristics, VGAE, SEAL — answers the *same* 1,054
questions. That sameness is not pedantry; it is what makes "0.897 beats
0.725" a fact rather than two papers shouting across incompatible
setups, and it is the first thing to check when reading anyone else's
link prediction table.

Two further choices define the evaluation. *Random vs temporal*: random
edge splits answer "which edges exist that I haven't looked at," while
temporal splits — train on edges before time $t$, test after — answer
"which edges will *form*," the question production actually asks; they
are harder, honester, and the default in industry (ogbn-arxiv's time
split from Lab 7 was this discipline for nodes; Week 14 makes it
strict for recommenders). Temporal splitting also dissolves a
philosophical awkwardness of random splits worth naming: a randomly
held-out edge *already existed* while the message graph was "current,"
so the random task is partly archaeology (find what we hid), while the
temporal task is genuine forecasting — and models can rank differently
across the two, because recency signals (new nodes, growing hubs)
matter only in the second. If your deployment forecasts, evaluate
forecasting.

*Metric* is the other axis, and it deserves numbers rather than vibes.
AUC asks "does a random true edge outscore a random false one" —
threshold-free, comparable, and blind to what deployments do, which is
*rank a shortlist*.

Feel the difference on a toy: 1,000 candidates, 10
true; model A gives every true edge rank 30–40 (AUC ≈ 0.97,
Hits@10 = 0); model B puts five true edges in the top ten and scatters
the rest to the bottom (lower AUC, Hits@10 = 0.5). A recommender ships
model B and a leaderboard crowns model A. Hits@K and MRR from Week 4
transfer verbatim and match products; report AUC for comparability,
Hits@K for truth, and distrust any table showing only the friendlier
one.

One vocabulary pair completes the setup, echoing Week 7: *transductive*
LP predicts missing edges among nodes seen in training (our Cora setup);
*inductive* LP scores pairs involving brand-new nodes — a new user, a
new molecule — where lookup-style embeddings forfeit (no row in the
table) and encoders that compute from features and neighborhoods are
mandatory. The Week 10 showdown's moral — encoders earn their keep
exactly where entities are new or feature-rich — applies to edges
unchanged.

## Stand on the heuristic floor

{{< include ../assets/d3/w12-heuristic.html >}}

The widget's ten hidden karate edges are the whole methodology in
miniature, and its verdict line is worth an honest look before the
formulas: common neighbors finds three of ten. Not eight — three. The
remaining seven hidden edges have few or no common neighbors in the
message graph (some *were* the only path between their endpoints), and
no triangle-closing formula can see them: recall has a structural
ceiling that no amount of formula polish lifts, which is the cleanest
argument for why learning enters at all. Keep that 3/10 in mind as the
Cora numbers arrive — AUC 0.724 sounds respectable precisely because
AUC averages over easy comparisons, while the widget's Hits-style count
tells you what a shortlist would actually contain.

Before learning anything, rank candidate pairs by a formula. The
classical ladder fits in one display:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CN}(a,b) &= |N(a) \cap N(b)|
&&\text{(common neighbors)}\\[2pt]
\mathrm{AA}(a,b) &= \textstyle\sum_{c \,\in\, N(a) \cap N(b)} \dfrac{1}{\log |N(c)|}
&&\text{(Adamic–Adar)}\\[2pt]
\mathrm{PA}(a,b) &= |N(a)| \cdot |N(b)|
&&\text{(preferential attachment)}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-w12-heuristics}

where —

- $a, b$ are the candidate pair's endpoints, and $N(\cdot)$ is a node's
  neighborhood *in the message graph only* — computing any of these on
  the full graph breaks the third rule of @def-w12-buckets;
- $c$ ranges over the common neighbors, and AA's $1 / \log|N(c)|$
  discounts the promiscuous ones: a shared appearance in a 4,000-member
  group means less than a shared collaborator — Week 2's degree
  skepticism, formulaized;
- **Jaccard** (not shown) divides CN by the union $|N(a) \cup N(b)|$;
  PA ignores overlap entirely and bets on rich-get-richer.

Measured on our Cora split: CN 0.724, AA 0.725. These
floors are not embarrassments to beat but *evidence about the task*:
they say most of Cora's link signal is triangle closure. When a task's
heuristics score high, learned models have little headroom (and a
heuristic serving at nanoseconds per pair may be the deployment answer);
when heuristics collapse — long-range links, bipartite graphs where CN
is structurally zero between users — that is precisely where learning
earns its keep. Run the floor first; it costs nothing and reads like a
diagnosis.

The family extends past two-hop formulas in directions you already own.
Katz scores ([Katz, 1953](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02289026)) sum
*all* paths between the pair with geometric damping —
Week 2's walk machinery as a similarity; personalized PageRank from $a$,
evaluated at $b$, does the same with the random surfer; both see beyond
common neighbors at the price of global computation. And the heuristics'
second career matters as much as their first: as *features*. A logistic
regression over {CN, AA, Jaccard, PA, Katz} is a strong, interpretable,
deployable model that many production link systems still run — and it
is the natural "shallow baseline" row for any deep table. Note also the
setting where the whole family goes structurally blind: bipartite
graphs. A user and an item can never share a neighbor (neighbors of
users are items and vice versa), so CN ≡ 0 across the prediction
boundary and the two-hop lens must widen to paths of length three —
which is precisely the door recommenders (Week 14) walk through.

<details>
<summary>Where this problem came from — one drawer of history</summary>
Link prediction predates deep learning by a comfortable margin.
[Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg's](https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.20591) 2003
study formalized the task on
co-authorship networks and benchmarked exactly the heuristics above —
their paper's ranking (Adamic–Adar surprisingly strong, preferential
attachment weak) still reproduces on our Cora split a generation of
methods later, which should calibrate your priors about progress. The
task then got an industry: friend suggestion at social networks
(People You May Know popularized triangle-closing at planetary scale),
and the Netflix Prize made "predict the missing user–item entry" the
decade's most famous ML problem — matrix factorization's finest hour,
and secretly bipartite link prediction with ratings. The GNN era
arrived in two steps you now recognize: GAE/VGAE (2016) put a learned
encoder under the dot product, and SEAL (2018) noticed that the *pair's
neighborhood* was the real signal and changed the object being
classified. The through-line of twenty years: better models moved the
number less than better evaluations moved the truth — the splits and
negatives of this lecture are where the field actually grew up.
</details>

## VGAE: the encoder meets a probabilistic decoder

The natural learned model reuses everything this course owns: encode
nodes with a GCN over the *message graph*, then score a pair by the
inner product —

$$
\hat p_{ab} \;=\; \operatorname{sigmoid}\!\big(z_a^\top z_b\big)
$$ {#eq-w12-decoder}

where —

- $z_a, z_b \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are the two endpoints' embeddings, read
  off the encoder's output;
- $z_a^\top z_b$ is their inner product — high when the encoder placed
  them nearby;
- $\operatorname{sigmoid}(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})$ squashes the score into
  $\hat p_{ab} \in (0,1)$, the predicted probability that edge $(a,b)$
  exists. (We spell the sigmoid out by name all week, because the
  symbol $\sigma$ has a second job coming: the latent standard
  deviation.)

This is Week 3's decoder with Week 6's encoder. The **graph
auto-encoder** (GAE) ([Kipf & Welling, 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07308))
is exactly that,
trained with binary cross-entropy on supervision positives against
sampled negatives, and it is worth pausing on what changed relative to
Week 3's pipeline, because the change is the whole point.
[DeepWalk's](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.6652)
embeddings were free parameters shaped by walk co-occurrence — the
graph entered only through which pairs the walks manufactured. Here the
embedding *is a function of features and neighborhood*, so two papers
with similar text and similar citers get similar embeddings even if no
walk ever connected them; the encoder generalizes across the graph
instead of memorizing per node — which is also, per the inductive
paragraph above, what lets it score pairs involving nodes born
tomorrow.

The **variational** upgrade treats each embedding as a distribution:
the encoder outputs a mean $\mu_v$ and a log-variance
$\log \sigma_v^2$ per node, and what flows to the decoder is a sample —

$$
z_v \;=\; \mu_v + \sigma_v \odot \epsilon,
\qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
$$ {#eq-w12-reparam}

where —

- $\mu_v, \sigma_v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are node $v$'s latent mean and
  standard deviation, two output heads of the same GCN encoder (from
  here on, a subscripted $\sigma$ is always this standard deviation and
  never the sigmoid of @eq-w12-decoder);
- $\odot$ is elementwise multiplication, and $\epsilon$ is a fresh
  standard-Gaussian noise vector, redrawn every forward pass;
- the arrangement is the **reparameterization trick**: the stochastic
  $z_v$ becomes a deterministic, differentiable function of
  $(\mu_v, \sigma_v)$ plus external noise — which is exactly what lets
  backprop assign credit through a sample.

The training objective is the ELBO:

::: {#def-w12-elbo .definition name="Evidence lower bound (ELBO), VGAE form"}
Training maximizes the **evidence lower bound**

$$
\mathcal{L} \;=\;
\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\big[\log p(A \mid Z)\big]
\;-\;
\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q(Z \mid X, A)\,\Vert\,\mathcal{N}(0, I)\big)
$$ {#eq-w12-elbo}

— a reconstruction term plus a KL term leashing the latent space toward
a standard Gaussian. Read it as one sentence: *explain the observed
edges, while claiming no more certainty than they justify.*
:::

where —

- $Z$ stacks the latent samples $z_v$; $X$ is the node-feature matrix
  and $A$ the (message-graph) adjacency;
- $q(Z \mid X, A)$ is the **variational posterior** — the encoder's
  per-node Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mu_v, \operatorname{diag}\sigma_v^2)$
  — and $\mathbb{E}_q$ averages over its samples (in practice, one
  reparameterized sample per training step);
- $p(A \mid Z)$ is the decoder's probability of the observed edges
  given the latents — @eq-w12-decoder applied pairwise;
- $\mathrm{KL}(\cdot \,\Vert\, \cdot)$ is the Kullback–Leibler
  divergence, the penalty for the posterior straying from the prior
  $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$.

What the leash buys:
regularization (embeddings cannot sprawl), calibrated uncertainty (a
node with contradictory neighborhoods gets honest variance rather than
a confident average), and a *generative* reading — sample $Z$ from the
prior, decode, and you have drawn a graph: the first hint of this
lecture's second half. Honesty compels the practical footnote the
original paper itself prints: on pure link prediction benchmarks GAE
and VGAE score within noise of each other — the variational machinery
earns its complexity when you *use* the distributionality (uncertainty,
generation, downstream Bayesian plumbing), not on AUC alone. Knowing
which upgrades are load-bearing for which purposes is, by Week 12,
simply how you read methods.

Walk the objective's two halves with formulas in hand, because Lab 12
makes you implement both. The reconstruction term treats every scored
pair as a Bernoulli:

$$
\log p(A \mid Z) \;=\;
\sum_{(a,b)} A_{ab} \log \hat p_{ab}
\;+\; (1 - A_{ab}) \log(1 - \hat p_{ab})
$$ {#eq-w12-recon}

where — $A_{ab} \in \{0, 1\}$ records whether the edge is observed,
$\hat p_{ab}$ is @eq-w12-decoder's probability, and the sum in
principle runs over all pairs $(a,b)$. In practice it runs over
supervision positives and sampled negatives rather than all $n^2$
pairs — the same sampled-softmax economics as Week 3, for the same
$O(n^2)$ reason. The KL term has a closed form for diagonal Gaussians,
per node:

$$
\mathrm{KL}_v \;=\;
-\tfrac12 \sum_{j=1}^{d}
\big(1 + \log\sigma_{vj}^2 - \mu_{vj}^2 - \sigma_{vj}^2\big)
$$ {#eq-w12-kl}

where — $j$ indexes the $d$ latent dimensions, and $\mu_{vj},
\sigma_{vj}$ are node $v$'s per-dimension latent mean and standard
deviation (Lab 12's `kl_term` docstring quotes this line verbatim). No
sampling is needed on this side: it is an analytic penalty pulling
every $\mu$ toward 0 and every $\sigma$ toward 1, and you can read its
gradient as "don't claim more certainty or more eccentricity than the
edges justify." The third ingredient, @eq-w12-reparam, you have already
met — and all three are reusable far beyond graphs: this is the
standard VAE toolkit, and meeting it here means you have now met it.

The three pieces assemble into a training step short enough to state
completely — and stating it pays, because Lab 12's third exercise is
this float line for line
([Kipf & Welling, 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07308)):

::: {#alg-w12-vgae .algorithm name="One VGAE Training Step"}
One gradient step on the ELBO, as Lab 12 implements it.

**Input:** features $X$; message graph $A_{\text{msg}}$; supervision
positives $P$; GCN encoder with mean and log-variance heads.
**Output:** updated encoder parameters.

1. $\mu, \log\sigma^2 \leftarrow \mathrm{GCN}(X, A_{\text{msg}})$ (two heads over a shared layer)
2. $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$; $Z \leftarrow \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon$ — @eq-w12-reparam
3. $N \leftarrow |P|$ non-edges sampled uniformly, all positives excluded
4. $\ell_{\text{rec}} \leftarrow$ cross-entropy of $z_a^\top z_b$: pairs in $P \to 1$, in $N \to 0$
5. $\ell_{\text{KL}} \leftarrow$ mean over nodes of @eq-w12-kl, scaled by $1/n$
6. backpropagate $\ell_{\text{rec}} + \ell_{\text{KL}}$; optimizer step
7. **return** (at evaluation: score pairs with $\mu$ alone — no sampling)
:::

Step 2 is what makes step 6 possible: gradients flow through the sample
because the randomness lives in $\epsilon$, not in the parameters. Step
4 is @eq-w12-recon in its sampled form; step 5's $1/n$ keeps the leash
proportionate to the reconstruction term ($n$ is the number of nodes).
And step 7's mean-only evaluation mirrors Week 11's rule — no sampling
at test time.

Measured, 200 epochs, 8 seconds: **AUC 0.903**, eighteen points over
the floor. Why does so simple a decoder do so well? Because Cora is
homophilous and the encoder is a GCN: two propagation layers pull
linked nodes' embeddings together *by construction*, so "high inner
product" and "nearby in the graph" become the same fact — the decoder
harvests what the encoder's inductive bias sowed. That reading also
predicts where the pipeline stalls: heterophilous links, structural
(rather than proximity) link rules, and anything where Week 9's
pair-blindness bites — the cue for SEAL. And here is the trained
object itself, decoded live — the actual 2-D latent of a VGAE we
trained on the karate club:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w12-vgae.html >}}

Carry over Week 4's discipline before admiring it: the inner-product
decoder is *symmetric* — $z_a^\top z_b = z_b^\top z_a$ — so VGAE cannot
express "a follows b but not conversely"; directed link prediction
needs the asymmetric decoders you already own (DistMult with source/
target roles, [ComplEx](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06357), translation
scores). The decoder zoo of Week 4
was never KG-specific; it was the menu of *pair-scoring functions*,
and this week finally says so out loud.

One more menu item earns a
mention because production uses it constantly: the **MLP decoder** —
concatenate $[z_a \Vert z_b]$ (or hand it $[z_a \Vert z_b \Vert z_a
\odot z_b \Vert |z_a - z_b|]$) and let a small network score the pair.
More expressive than any fixed form, trivially made asymmetric or
symmetric by construction, and the default head in most applied link
systems; its cost is that the beautiful geometric readings of Week 4
(translation, rotation) dissolve into weights.

## SEAL: when the pair's *structure* is the signal

Something is conceptually wrong with every dot-product method, and Week
9 taught you the vocabulary to say it precisely. Node embeddings are
computed *per node*; the pair's score is assembled afterwards. Now take
two candidate pairs $(a, b)$ and $(a, c)$ where $b$ and $c$ are
structurally interchangeable — automorphic twins, Week 9's
indistinguishable nodes. Any encoder that respects the graph's symmetry
assigns $z_b = z_c$, hence identical scores — even if $b$ shares three
common neighbors with $a$ and $c$ shares none, because *which* neighbors
are shared is a property of the pair, not of either endpoint.

This is not a contrived worry, and you can verify it on the course's
oldest friend. The karate club contains genuine twins: nodes **14, 15,
18, 20, and 22** all have exactly the neighborhood $\{32, 33\}$ — five
structurally identical wallflowers — and nodes **17 and 21** share
$\{0, 1\}$. Every symmetric featureless encoder in this course
(uniform-feature GCN, walk embeddings in expectation) gives all five
wallflowers one embedding, so for *any* anchor $a$, the five candidate
pairs $(a, 14), (a, 15), \dots$ receive one score — even though $a=33$
is already linked to all five while a rival anchor might share both,
one, or neither of their neighbors. Whatever the truth is, a per-node
embedding cannot spell it: pair prediction from unconditioned node
embeddings is structurally lossy.

The labeling-trick paper
([Zhang et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.16103), optional
reading) turned this observation into theorems — and into a family of
fixes (identity-aware and labeling GNNs) of which SEAL is the founding
member.

SEAL's repair is to change the object being classified — and the shape
of the move deserves a beat of recognition before the mechanics,
because you have seen it twice. Week 9's route past the WL ceiling was
"give the nodes structural features the message passing can't compute";
Week 10's HAN gave each metapath its own view; SEAL gives each *pair*
its own view — the same maneuver, one level up: when the architecture
cannot condition on the thing that matters, move the thing that matters
into the input. The labeling-trick literature calls the general pattern
*structural conditioning*, and once you can name it you will spot it in
subgraph GNNs, in identity-aware architectures, and in every "add a
marker token" trick the transformer world uses for the same reason:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w12-seal.html >}}

::: {#def-w12-labeling .definition name="Enclosing subgraph and the labeling trick"}
For a candidate pair $(a, b)$, the **enclosing subgraph** is everything
within $k$ hops of either endpoint, with the candidate edge itself
removed *everywhere* — from the subgraph's edges and from every
structure the labels are computed from. The **labeling trick** then
assigns each node in it a structural feature — its pair of distances
to the two endpoints — before any learning happens. The object being
classified is no longer a pair of node embeddings but a small labeled
graph; that relocation is the entire architectural move.
:::

The procedure, formalized — and matched line for line to Lab 12's
`node_labels(nodes, a, b, leak=False)`, whose `leak` switch you will
throw on purpose
([Zhang & Chen, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.09691)):

::: {#alg-w12-seal .algorithm name="SEAL: Extract, Label, Classify"}
Score a candidate edge by classifying its labeled neighborhood.

**Input:** message-graph adjacency sets $\mathrm{adj}$; candidate pair
$(a, b)$; hop budget $k$; a small GNN classifier.
**Output:** a score for the candidate edge $(a, b)$.

1. $\mathrm{adj}_a \leftarrow \mathrm{adj}[a] \setminus \{b\}$; $\mathrm{adj}_b \leftarrow \mathrm{adj}[b] \setminus \{a\}$ — the leak line
2. $V_s \leftarrow \{a, b\} \,\cup\,$ all nodes within $k$ hops of $a$ or $b$
3. $E_s \leftarrow$ message-graph edges among $V_s$, minus $(a, b)$ itself
4. **for** each node $v \in V_s$ **do**
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$d_a \leftarrow \min(\mathrm{dist}(v, a), 2)$; $d_b \leftarrow \min(\mathrm{dist}(v, b), 2)$, from $\mathrm{adj}_a, \mathrm{adj}_b$
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$x_v \leftarrow$ one-hot of the pair $(d_a, d_b)$ — a common neighbor wears $(1,1)$
7. **end for**
8. **return** $\mathrm{GNN}(V_s, E_s, \{x_v\})$, pooled to one logit
:::

Step 1 is the week's centerpiece and the entire content of our 0.363:
the candidate edge must vanish from the *adjacency sets* the distance
labels read (`adj_a = adj[a] - {b}` in the lab), not merely from the
subgraph's edge list — step 3 alone is not enough. Lab 12's
`leak=True` switch is precisely "skip step 1"; every other line stays
identical, and that one skipped line is the difference between 0.897
and 0.363. Steps 4–6 cost one truncated distance check per node
(distances capped at 2, so endpoints read 0, their neighbors 1,
everything else 2); step 8 is an ordinary two-layer GIN over a few
dozen nodes. Our SEAL-lite runs the float with $k = 1$.

The labels break the symmetry **relative to the pair**: the same node
$c$ gets different labels in different candidates' subgraphs, which is
exactly the pair-conditioning that per-node embeddings lack — the
karate twins, finally distinguishable. And every heuristic becomes
learnable: counting $(1,1)$ nodes is common neighbors
(@eq-w12-heuristics, first line); weighting them by degree is
Adamic–Adar; the GNN can learn those and whatever else the subgraph
holds.

The anatomy of our 0.363, step by step, because the mechanism
generalizes to every leak you will ever hunt. With the target edge
still inside the adjacency sets, node $a$'s label in a *training*
positive's subgraph came out $(0, 1)$ — "I am endpoint one, and I am
adjacent to endpoint two" — while in every *negative*'s subgraph it
came out $(0, 2)$. A perfectly separating feature, visible to a GIN in
one epoch; training accuracy sailed to 100%.

But *test* positives had
their edges properly excluded from the message graph, so their
endpoints also read $(0, 2)$ — the same signature as negatives — and
the model, having staked everything on the leaked bit, confidently
scored test positives *as negatives*: AUC 0.363, which is 0.637 with
the sign flipped. Every symptom was textbook: implausibly fast training
convergence, a train–test gap wider than the model's capacity explains,
and sub-coin test performance — three tripwires you can now name, and
the last one is the gift, because a merely-useless model scores 0.5;
only a *leak-trained* model scores meaningfully below it.

Measured, leak-free: **0.897** — and the number needs its honest
footnote. Our deliberately budget SEAL-lite — 1-hop subgraphs,
distances capped at 2, eight epochs — *ties* VGAE (0.897 vs 0.903)
rather than beating it, because on homophilous Cora the encoder already
captures most of the proximity signal, and our truncated labels capture
little more than common-neighbor counts. The full SEAL recipe — 2-hop
extraction, exact double-radius labels, deeper nets, and crucially the
harder benchmarks where proximity is *not* the story — is where its
advantage over dot products becomes decisive and where it still anchors
leaderboards. As always: the architecture's edge is task-shaped, and
the measured tie is itself information about Cora. The ladder, in one
figure — including the row this lecture opened with:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w12-ladder.html >}}

## Negatives are a design surface, not a formality

Between the models and the metrics sits a decision this lecture has so
far waved through: *which non-edges do you score against?* It deserves
its own section because it silently controls every number on every
table, in evaluation and in training separately.

|  | **uniform non-edges** | **hard negatives** |
|---|---|---|
| **evaluation** (sets the exam) | the literature's default: cheap comparisons, flattering AUC | degree-matched or retrieval near-misses: numbers drop, rankings can flip |
| **training** (sets the curriculum) | unbiased but lazy gradients after epoch one | fast teacher, risky syllabus — a near-true "negative" may be true |

: Negative sampling is two independent design decisions, and each cell trades honesty against convenience differently. {#tbl-w12-negatives}

**Evaluation negatives** set the exam's difficulty. Uniform non-edges —
our protocol, and the literature's default — are mostly trivial: two
random Cora papers share nothing, and outscoring them is cheap, which
is partly why every method looks strong on AUC. Harder, honester
choices: *degree-matched* negatives (sample non-edges whose endpoint
degrees mirror the positives', so the model cannot win on "these nodes
are active" alone) and *retrieval negatives* (score against the
candidates an actual retrieval system would surface — the near-misses).
Expect absolute numbers to drop sharply under harder negatives; expect
*rankings between methods* to sometimes flip, because heuristics and
dot products lean on degree signals precisely the hard negatives
neutralize. A result that survives negative-hardening is a result.

**Training negatives** shape what the model learns, and the trade is
the one Week 4 taught with self-adversarial sampling: uniform negatives
give unbiased but lazy gradients (most are too easy to teach anything
after epoch one); hard negatives teach fast but risk teaching wrong
(a "hard negative" adjacent to being true may *be* true — the
accidentally-true problem, sharpened). Production recommenders resolve
this with in-batch negatives (other users' positives double as your
negatives — cheap, moderately hard, slightly biased) plus a sprinkle of
mined hard negatives, and Week 14 will show this machinery deployed.
For the lab and this lecture, uniform-with-exclusions is the correct
*starting* protocol — simple, reproducible, comparable — with
negative-hardening as the stress test you run before believing
yourself.

## Graphs from nothing

Prediction fills holes in a given graph; **generation** asks for new
graphs outright. The applications are not exotic, and each imposes its
own definition of success. Molecular design is the flagship: generate
candidate molecules whose graphs satisfy chemistry (valence rules —
*validity*), that aren't copies of the training set (*novelty*) or of
each other (*uniqueness*), and whose property distributions —
synthesizability, solubility, drug-likeness — sit where the designer
aims; every serious molecular generator reports that metric quartet,
and DiGress's headline results are exactly there.

Synthetic data is
the second industry: share a realistic-but-fake network when the real
one is private — with the honesty footnote that generation is not
automatically anonymization: a generator that memorizes can leak real
edges into its samples, and membership-style audits (is this training
edge suspiciously frequent in samples?) belong in any privacy claim.
Then stress testing (feed your pipeline graphs whose properties you
control), augmentation, and simulation. The technical obstacle
underneath all of them is one you have met twice: a graph has no
canonical order (Week 6's permutation lesson), yet sequence models
need one, and the output space is $O(n^2)$ discrete decisions that
must *cohere* — triangles, valences, communities are properties of
decision *sets*, not single entries.

**GraphRNN** ([You et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08773))
answers with autoregression under a chosen order:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w12-generate.html >}}

Fix a BFS ordering of the training graph's nodes (BFS is the masterstroke:
it guarantees each new node's edges reach only a bounded recent window
of $M$ predecessors — $M$ is the *BFS window width*, ours is 12 —
collapsing the $O(n^2)$ decisions to $O(nM)$), then
generate node by node: a graph-level RNN carries the history; per node, a
row of edge decisions to the recent window is emitted — call that row
$S_i \in \{0, 1\}^M$, node $i$'s edge indicators to its $M$ most recent
predecessors in the ordering. (The full model
uses a second, edge-level RNN so the decisions within a row condition on
each other; our budget GraphRNN-S emits them independently — a
simplification that costs correlation *within* a row and buys a model
you can read in twenty lines — and which still, as the measurements
below show, learns the community signature that the independence-only
ER baseline cannot fake, which is itself a small lesson in how much of
a distribution the *history conditioning alone* carries.)

Training penalizes each predicted row with per-entry binary
cross-entropy, under the standard autoregressive regime:

::: {#def-w12-teacherforcing .definition name="Teacher forcing"}
Train an autoregressive model by feeding the *true* previous step as
input — here, the true row $S_{i-1}$ — and penalizing its prediction
of the current step $S_i$, so the model never sees its own mistakes
during training. Optimization stays stable; the price is **exposure
bias** — at generation time the model must condition on its own,
possibly drifting, samples — a caveat imported wholesale from language
modeling.
:::

The mechanics on
our data: two hundred graphs of 12–20 nodes, BFS window $M{=}12$,
hidden state 64, sixty epochs in **23 seconds**, final per-entry loss
0.102 — small enough numbers that Lab 12 has you retrain it from
scratch and beat the baseline yourself. Generation then runs the loop
open: start from a start-of-sequence row, sample each row from the
emitted Bernoullis, feed the *sample* back, stop at the target size —
autoregression's standard trick pair (teach on truth, generate on
self), and the moment where the ordering choice silently matters again:
the model generates in BFS-like orders because those are the only
orders it ever saw.

**Diffusion** (DiGress —
[Vignac et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.14734), optional
reading) answers orderlessly: corrupt
training graphs step by step toward noise, train a network to reverse
one corruption step, then generate by denoising pure noise — all edges
decided *jointly and iteratively* rather than sequentially, no ordering
ever chosen, permutation equivariance holding by construction. The
adjective *discrete* is DiGress's actual contribution and worth one
careful sentence: naive graph diffusion adds Gaussian noise to the
adjacency matrix, wandering through meaningless fractional "edges,"
while DiGress corrupts *categorically* — each edge slot hops between
{no-edge, single, double, aromatic…} under a transition matrix, each
node between atom types — so every intermediate step is a legal
discrete graph and the denoiser (a graph transformer, next week's
protagonist making an early entrance) always works on well-typed
objects. It leads molecule generation benchmarks; its price is
hundreds of denoising passes per sample and a heavier model — the
classic diffusion trade, unchanged from images.

Which paradigm when? Autoregression samples fast (one pass), streams
naturally, and inherits ordering artifacts; diffusion samples slowly,
scales awkwardly past hundreds of nodes, and owns the quality crown on
small structured graphs like molecules. And both share a ceiling this
course can name: the *evaluator* — next paragraph — is weaker than
either generator, which is an uncomfortable place for a field to
stand.

And how do you *grade* a generator? You cannot ask "is this sample
correct" — novelty is the point. The field's answer: compare
*distributions of statistics* between generated and held-out graphs.
The GraphRNN paper's protocol, still standard: collect each graph's
degree distribution, clustering-coefficient distribution, and
four-node *orbit* counts (how often each node sits in each position of
each 4-node motif — graphlets from Week 2, promoted to evaluator), then
measure distance between the generated set's statistics and the test
set's with maximum mean discrepancy — a kernel two-sample distance
whose one-line intuition is "embed both empirical distributions and
measure the gap."

Our lab keeps the protocol and swaps MMD for the
friendlier total-variation distance on histograms — same
question, simpler estimator, and the *comparative* conclusions (model
vs baseline) come out the same, which for a course beats a formula
you'd treat as a black box. Measured: our GraphRNN's samples sit at TV 0.111 (degree)
and 0.154 (clustering) from held-out community graphs, while
density-matched ER baselines sit at 0.152 and **0.596** — the ER graphs
have the right amount of edges and no idea that triangles live inside
communities. Judge for yourself, on the real samples:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w12-generate.html >}}

Close the loop with Week 9 before moving on, because the evaluation has
a principled blind spot: two very different graphs can share degree and
clustering histograms — statistics-matching is *necessary, not
sufficient*, the WL lesson wearing an evaluator's badge. Serious
molecule work therefore adds validity/uniqueness/novelty checks and
task-specific property distributions; and every generation paper's
metrics section deserves the same skepticism you now apply to
leaderboards.

Where did this line of work go after 2018? Into chemistry's toolchain,
mostly. The GraphRNN idea grew constraint-aware descendants that
generate molecules atom-by-atom under valence rules; a reinforcement
learning layer was bolted on top to steer samples toward desired
properties (generate, score with a property predictor, reward the
generator — with the amusing failure mode that the generator learns to
fool the *predictor* rather than the chemistry, adversarial examples in
reverse); scaffold-constrained variants grow decorations around a fixed
core the medicinal chemists refuse to negotiate.

Diffusion currently
owns the unconditional-quality crown; autoregression still owns speed
and streaming. The professional summary you should retain: in
generation, the generator is rarely the bottleneck anymore — the
*property predictor* and the *evaluation protocol* are, which is why a
course that overtrained you on evaluation discipline has been secretly
preparing you for this field too.

## The method: a link prediction experiment that survives review

The week's checklist, in the order that catches bugs cheapest:

**Build the split first, audit it second.** Four buckets, one job per
edge; assert programmatically that test ∩ message = ∅ and that negatives
avoid all positives (Lab 12's validator is twelve lines and has already
caught one real leak this week — ours). Write the auditor before the
model, the way you write a test before a bug exists: split code is
written once and trusted for months, which is exactly the profile of
code that deserves its asserts up front.

**Run the heuristic ladder.** CN and AA on the message graph. Their
scores calibrate everything above them; if AA hits 0.95, question the
task before celebrating any model.

**Match the metric to the product.** Ranking product → Hits@K/MRR with
realistic candidate sets; scientific comparison → AUC as well. Report
both; distrust papers that report only the friendlier one.

**Then model, cheapest first.** GAE/VGAE (an afternoon), SEAL where pair
structure plausibly matters, and the decoder chosen for the relation's
symmetry (Week 4's menu). Every step compared against the floor, with
the same negatives.

**Interrogate suspicious success.** Any jump that looks too good gets
the leak audit: recompute labels/features with the target edge removed
*everywhere*; rerun with temporal splits if time exists; check the
negatives for accidental positives. Our 0.363 was caught precisely
because a "too clean" training curve met an inverted test score — treat
disagreement between train and test as a *tripwire*, not noise.

Watch the checklist run once on a fresh brief: *a university wants
collaborator suggestions from its co-authorship graph.*

| checklist step | decision for this brief |
|---|---|
| split | temporal — train on collaborations before 2024, test on 2024–25 pairs; the product forecasts, so the eval must |
| audit | assert no post-2023 edge in the message graph; features like "shared coauthors" computed *as of the cutoff* |
| floor | AA on the pre-2024 graph (expect strong — co-authorship closes triangles ferociously; if AA alone hits 0.9, a heuristic-plus-features logistic model may be the deliverable) |
| metric | the UI shows five suggestions — Hits@5 against retrieval-realistic negatives, AUC in the appendix |
| models | VGAE-style encoder for the many new-faculty (inductive) cases; SEAL where the floor left headroom |
| leak check | any AUC above ~0.95 on co-authorship triggers the audit reflex — that number usually means a feature saw the future |

: The five-step method, run on a one-page design. Total design time: one page — and every choice traceable to a sentence in this lecture, which is what "method" means here. {#tbl-w12-brief}

One synthesis before the pitfalls, because this week quietly completed
a unification the course began in September. Week 3 scored node pairs
with a dot product and called it link prediction. Week 4 replaced the
dot product with a *menu* of pair-scorers — translations, bilinear
forms, rotations — chosen by the relation's algebra. Week 10 put a
learned encoder under that menu and measured when it paid. This week
added the last two entries: the *variational* scorer (VGAE — a
distribution over embeddings under the same inner product) and the
*pair-conditioned* scorer (SEAL — where the "embedding" is computed
fresh for each candidate, with the pair baked into the features).

One
task, five decoder generations, and a single organizing question you
can now ask of any link system in one breath: *what function scores a
pair, what can that function not express, and was anything it reads
computed in a world where the answer was already written down?* The
first two clauses are Weeks 3–12 of representation theory; the third is
Weeks 1–12 of evaluation discipline; and the exam will ask all three.

## Common pitfalls

**Evaluating on edges the model propagated over.** The classic. If test
edges live in the message graph, walks and messages deliver the answers
— +17 AUC of fiction, measured in Week 3, re-measured every year by
somebody's retracted table. The subtle variant: an *encoder trained
long ago* on the full graph, reused for "a quick link experiment" —
pretrained embeddings carry their training graph's edges inside them
forever, and provenance amnesia is how careful people leak.

**Removing the target edge from the graph but not the features.** Our
0.363. Distance labels, common-neighbor counts, any feature computed
from adjacency must be computed *as if the candidate edge does not
exist* — for negatives too (they never had it; positives must match).

**Negatives that are secretly positives.** Sampling "random pairs" that
include validation/test edges teaches the model that true edges are
false and grades it against poisoned keys. Exclude *all* positive sets
— and in temporal settings, remember that a pair negative today may be
positive next month, which is not a bug but a property of the task:
"negative" in link prediction always means "not yet observed," Week 4's
open-world assumption in one more costume.

**AUC-only reporting on ranking products.** AUC 0.90 can coexist with
Hits@10 that embarrasses a heuristic — the metric averages over vast
irrelevant score space, and our toy model-A/model-B example earlier in
the lecture is not hypothetical: it is the shape of several real
recommender post-mortems. If the product shows ten slots, measure ten
slots.

**Trusting sample-vs-sample eyeballing for generators.** Individual
samples always look plausible; distributions expose the fraud. And
matched statistics still aren't identity — keep Week 9 in the room.

**Computing "as-of" features with today's graph.** In temporal setups,
every feature — shared neighbors, degrees, PageRank — must be computed
from the graph *as of the training cutoff*. Recomputing on the current
graph quietly imports the future; it is the single most common leak in
industrial link systems because the feature store updates nightly and
nobody told the offline evaluation.

## Required reading

- **[Kipf & Welling — Variational Graph Auto-Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07308)**
  (NeurIPS BDL
  2016). Two pages that launched a subfield — a useful genre lesson in
  itself: a workshop note with one clean idea, cited tens of thousands
  of times. Derive the ELBO alongside §2, note what the inner-product
  decoder can't say, and notice the paper's own GAE-vs-VGAE table
  showing the honesty this lecture repeated.
- **[Zhang & Chen — Link Prediction Based on GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.09691)**
  (NeurIPS 2018).
  SEAL. Read §3 for extraction and the double-radius labeling function
  (our lab's labels are its min(·,2) truncation), and the γ-decaying
  theorem connecting enclosing subgraphs to the whole high-order
  heuristic family — the result that says "the subgraph contains every
  formula from this lecture's floor."
- **[You et al. — GraphRNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08773)**
  (ICML 2018). The BFS insight (§2.3) is the
  paper; the two-level RNN and the MMD evaluation protocol complete
  it. Their appendix's baseline zoo (ER, BA, Kronecker) is a model of
  how to position a generator against classical random-graph theory.

Optional: the [labeling-trick paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.16103)
(NeurIPS 2021) for the theory of
multi-node representations — the formal version of this lecture's
karate-twins argument, and worth reading just for how a folk
observation becomes a theorem;
[DiGress](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.14734) (ICLR 2023) for discrete
diffusion done properly, including the marginal-preserving noise
schedule that makes the intermediate graphs realistic; the
[TKDE survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15617)
(2024) for the diffusion family map when you need to place a new
generation paper in thirty seconds.

## Check your understanding

**Q1.** Your pipeline computes each node's PageRank on the full graph as
a feature, then predicts test edges. Name the leak, its Week-2
mechanism, and the fix.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
PageRank flows along *all* edges — including test edges, whose presence
perturbs scores of their endpoints; the feature smuggles test adjacency
into training. Fix: compute every structural feature on the message
graph only (and for candidate-conditioned features, with the candidate
removed). Same family as our 0.363: features must live in the world where
the answer is unknown.
</details>

**Q2.** Derive why GAE's inner-product decoder cannot beat 50% AUC on
the task "predict the direction of an edge known to exist."

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Direction prediction scores $(a, b)$ against $(b, a)$; the decoder
gives $\operatorname{sigmoid}(z_a^\top z_b) =
\operatorname{sigmoid}(z_b^\top z_a)$ — identical scores
for every pair by symmetry of the inner product, so every comparison is
a tie and AUC is exactly 0.5. The fix is Week 4's menu: any asymmetric
pair-scorer (source/target embeddings, DistMult-with-roles, ComplEx,
translations).
</details>

**Q3.** In SEAL's subgraph for candidate $(a,b)$, what labels do: a
common neighbor; a neighbor of $a$ only; the node $a$ itself? And why
must the same physical node relabel across different candidates?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Common neighbor $(1,1)$; $a$-only neighbor $(1,2)$; $a$ itself $(0,2)$
— the second coordinate computed with the candidate edge deleted from
the adjacency sets, so $a$ is no longer adjacent to $b$ (skip that
deletion and $a$ reads $(0,1)$ for training positives only: the leak). Relabeling across candidates is the entire point: labels encode
position *relative to the pair*, giving the GNN pair-conditioned inputs
that unconditioned node embeddings provably cannot supply (automorphic
twins get equal embeddings but different labels).
</details>

**Q4.** Why does GraphRNN use a BFS ordering rather than a random
permutation, quantitatively?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Under BFS, a new node's neighbors all lie within a bounded recent
window of the ordering (a BFS frontier is contiguous), so each row of
edge decisions has width $M \ll n$: sequence length drops from
$O(n^2)$ to $O(nM)$, training sees vastly fewer orderings (BFS orders
are a tiny subset of all $n!$), and the RNN's memory burden shrinks
accordingly. Random orderings scatter a node's edges across the whole
history — the model must remember everything forever, and mostly
fails to.
</details>

**Q5.** Our GraphRNN beat ER by 0.04 TV on degree but by 0.44 on
clustering. Explain the asymmetry and what it says about ER as a
baseline.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
ER with matched density gets the *mean* degree right for free — degree
histograms of sparse ER are Poisson-ish and roughly landable — but ER
edges are independent, so triangles occur at chance rates: community
graphs' high within-block clustering is exactly what independence
cannot fake. Degree statistics are a weak discriminator (most
generators pass); higher-order structure is where generative quality
actually shows — choose evaluation statistics that your naive baseline
fails, or the comparison certifies nothing.
</details>

**Q6.** A paper reports link prediction AUC 0.96 with negatives sampled
uniformly from non-edges. The product retrieves 10 candidates per user
from millions. Name two reasons the number may not survive contact.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Uniform negatives are mostly absurdly easy (random pairs share
nothing); ranking a true edge above them is cheap, and AUC averages
over exactly those easy comparisons. Deployment ranks against *hard*
negatives — plausible near-misses surfaced by retrieval — and shows
only 10 slots, so Hits@10 against hard negatives is the honest number
and typically far lower. (Degree-matched or in-batch negatives are the
standard patch; Week 14 does this properly for recommenders.)
</details>

**Q7.** Sketch the VGAE loss and say precisely what breaks if you (a)
drop the KL term, (b) drop the reparameterization and sample directly.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(A \mid Z)] - \mathrm{KL}(q(Z \mid
X, A) \Vert \mathcal{N}(0, I))$. (a) Without KL it is a plain GAE with
noise: variances inflate or collapse unregularized, the latent space
loses its prior geometry, and sampling-from-prior generation stops
being meaningful. (b) Sampling $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$
directly is non-differentiable w.r.t. $(\mu, \sigma)$ — gradients
cannot flow into the encoder; reparameterization moves the randomness
into $\epsilon$ so the sample is a deterministic, differentiable
function of the parameters.
</details>

**Q8.** Design the three-line audit that would have caught our 0.363
before any training run.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
For a handful of *training positives*, compute the pair's features/
labels twice — once normally, once with the pair's edge force-removed
from every adjacency structure — and assert they are identical; repeat
for test positives and assert the same distributions. Our bug fails
the first assert instantly (training positives' endpoint labels change
when the edge is removed; test positives' don't), no GPU required.
Generalization: any feature of a supervised pair must be invariant to
that pair's own label.
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **the four-bucket split** (@def-w12-buckets) — message / supervision /
  validation / test: one job per edge, every leak a violated card.
- **heuristic floor** (@eq-w12-heuristics) — CN, AA, PA ranked before any
  learning; Cora's floor is 0.724, and it is the baseline, not the coin.
- **ELBO** (@def-w12-elbo) — reconstruction minus KL: explain the edges,
  claim no extra certainty.
- **reparameterization trick** (@eq-w12-reparam) — randomness moved into
  $\epsilon$ so gradients flow through a sample.
- **enclosing subgraph & labeling trick** (@def-w12-labeling) — classify
  the pair's neighborhood; labels are distances to the endpoints, and
  step 1 of @alg-w12-seal is the leak-proofing.
- **negatives as a design surface** (@tbl-w12-negatives) — evaluation
  negatives set the exam, training negatives the curriculum.
- **teacher forcing & exposure bias** (@def-w12-teacherforcing) — train
  on truth, generate on self.
- **BFS window** — GraphRNN's $M$: the bound that collapses $O(n^2)$
  edge decisions to $O(nM)$.
- **statistics-based evaluation** — TV/MMD between distributions of
  degree, clustering, orbits; necessary, never sufficient — Week 9's
  lesson wearing an evaluator's badge.
:::

## Where this leaves us

The task flipped and the discipline held: four buckets with one job per
edge, a heuristic floor before any learning (0.724), an encoder-decoder
that reused six weeks of parts (0.903), a labeling trick that
conditions on the pair (0.897) — and a one-line leak that turned the
same model into an anti-predictor (0.363), caught by the audit this
course has been drilling since Week 1. Then graphs from nothing:
autoregression with a clever ordering, diffusion without one, and
generators graded by the statistics of their offspring — with the
karate club's five wallflower twins as the standing reminder of what
per-node embeddings can never say about a pair, and the ER baseline's
0.596 clustering miss as the standing reminder that a generator is
judged against a null model, never against applause.

Bank the transferables, because they outlast every model named today:
the four-bucket reflex; the heuristic-floor-first habit; the
"features must live in the world where the answer is unknown"
invariant, which generalizes far beyond graphs; the metric-matches-
the-product rule; and the null-model instinct for anything generative.
Every one of them will appear on the final in some costume.

Close the loop — one minute, no notes, per this course's custom, and
this week's reconstruction has four stations: the four buckets and
which rule our 0.363 broke; the karate twins and why dot products
cannot tell their pairs apart; the ELBO's two terms and what each one
disciplines; and the BFS window that makes GraphRNN's sequence length
linear. Whichever resists reconstruction is tonight's reread — and the
0.363 story specifically is one to rehearse until you can tell it at a
whiteboard in ninety seconds, because you will spend some part of your
career telling exactly that story to a team that doesn't yet believe
its beautiful number is a leak.

And carry one thread forward. SEAL won by *reading structure around a
pair* — but its GNN is still message passing, still Week 9's prisoner:
local, oversquashed at range, blind above 1-WL. Next week the
architecture itself mutinies: attention over *all* node pairs at once,
no edges required — the transformer, arriving on graphs with positional
encodings you already hold (Week 9's RW returns, Week 6's
eigenvectors) doing the work adjacency used to do. The recipe that
finally beat message passing on molecules is one part attention, one
part MPNN, and two parts the structural and positional features this
course has been quietly stockpiling all semester — which is to say,
next week you arrive already owning most of the ingredients.
